strengths: Soundness/idea: ASTRA addresses a genuine systems bottleneck by retaining full-precision local attention while vector-quantizing remote token embeddings. The number of quantization groups provides a simple, useful accuracy–communication trade-off.

Evaluation breadth: The study covers ViT-Base, GPT-2 Small/Medium, four datasets, multiple bandwidths, device counts, and sequence lengths. Component ablations support the empirical usefulness of noise augmentation and distributed class tokens.

Significance: Enabling collaborative inference at low bandwidth could be valuable for edge deployments. The reported accuracy and latency results are promising enough to motivate further investigation.
Presentation: The main algorithm and motivation are generally easy to follow, and the latency breakdowns and accuracy/communication tables communicate the intended trade-offs clearly.
Limitations and ethics: The authors candidly report the substantial zero-shot language-modeling degradation and discuss reliability and maintenance concerns in distributed deployments.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 1 is not valid as stated. From X = X_hat + epsilon, the manuscript asserts Cov(X) = Cov(X_hat) + Cov(epsilon), omitting cross-covariance terms. It then applies the closed-form Gaussian Wasserstein formula even though X is not assumed Gaussian and X_hat is a discrete quantized distribution. The later iid isotropic-Gaussian assumption is absent from the theorem, and strict inequality can also fail in degenerate cases.

Soundness: Theorem 2 likewise does not establish its claimed exact 1/N error reduction. Softmax perturbations are coupled rather than mutually independent; errors across devices share quantized tokens and need not be independent or identically distributed; variance bounds are converted into equalities; and the derivation confuses the number of non-local tokens with output coordinates. A first-order approximation cannot justify the exact theorem stated for the full attention computation.

Evidence for the central systems claim is insufficiently specified. The paper says distributed inference is simulated on laptops with 1660Ti GPUs and bandwidth caps, but does not clearly distinguish measured execution from analytically added communication time or describe topology, collectives, serialization, synchronization, packet latency, or bandwidth-control methodology. Only means over 20 runs are reported, without variance or tail latency.

Communication accounting is ambiguous and potentially optimistic. The tabulated 120 bits per token equals 10 bits times 12 layers and apparently omits the replication/routing factor needed to deliver an index to N-1 peers. The paper also does not explain practical 10-bit packing, collective-protocol traffic, class-token aggregation, codebook access, or whether nearest-codeword search and decoding overhead are included.

The GPT evaluation supports only prefill acceleration: autoregressive decoding is explicitly moved to one device. No complete generation latency is measured as a function of output length, despite broad claims about Transformer inference. For many interactive language-model workloads decoding dominates end-to-end latency.

Accuracy comparisons and reproducibility details are incomplete. It is unclear whether the original models receive an exactly matched fine-tuning budget; the authors report the best beta setting without a clearly separated model-selection protocol; and learning rates, batch sizes, schedules, sequence lengths, codebook initialization sample counts, seeds, and uncertainty across runs are missing. The abstract says the system is open-sourced, but the supplied manuscript contains no repository link.

Significance is limited by evaluation on only homogeneous, older consumer GPUs and relatively small/base models. There is no real wireless experiment, heterogeneous-device study, failure/straggler analysis, energy measurement, or evaluation of larger modern language models and KV-cache behavior.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: compressing communicated activations with vector quantization is a natural extension of sequence parallelism, while noise augmentation and replicated class-token averaging are incremental. The invalid theoretical results currently weaken the claimed new understanding behind both additions.

Presentation has several avoidable ambiguities and errors, including inconsistent headline speedups (2.64 versus plotted/described 2.65–2.74), a table described as showing up to 15.25x improvement while it contains much larger ratios against TP/SP, and recurrent typographical issues. The limitations discussion also omits privacy leakage from exchanged quantized representations and security implications of collaborative devices.

strengths: Significance: The paper addresses a relevant bottleneck—communication during sequence-parallel inference on bandwidth-constrained devices—and the proposed accuracy/communication trade-off could be practically useful.

Empirical scope: The evaluation covers ViT-Base, GPT2-Small, and GPT2-Medium, vision and language tasks, 2–8 devices, 10–500 Mbps, and sequences up to 4096 tokens. Tables 1–3 expose the trade-off rather than reporting speed alone; for example, 32-group ASTRA reaches 91.64% versus 92.53% on CIFAR-100 and 80.05% versus 80.32% on ImageNet-1K.

Presentation: The high-level mechanism is understandable. Figure 2 clearly illustrates local full-precision versus remote quantized tokens, and the latency breakdowns help communicate the intended systems advantage.

Limitations and ethics: The authors honestly report the substantial zero-shot degradation, increased codebook storage, and reliability risks of distributed deployment. These disclosures are appropriate and should not themselves be penalized; no major unresolved ethical concern is apparent.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 1 is not established. From X = X-hat + epsilon, the proof asserts C_X = C_X-hat + Sigma while omitting cross-covariance terms between X-hat and epsilon. It then applies the closed-form Gaussian Wasserstein formula although neither X nor X-hat is assumed Gaussian. The later iid isotropic residual assumption is absent from the theorem statement and still does not repair these issues. Even strict inequality fails in degenerate cases. Thus the claimed theoretical justification for noise augmentation is false as stated.

Soundness: Theorem 2 is also unsupported. Softmax perturbations are declared mutually independent even though they share the term sum_k alpha_k e_k. Errors from different devices are likewise not independent because their class tokens use overlapping quantized tokens. Equations 30–31 additionally confuse the number of non-local tokens with output coordinates and promote a first-order approximation into an exact 1/N equality. This invalidates a prominently claimed justification for distributed class tokens.

Soundness: Equation 1 multiplies logits by a mask before softmax. A binary multiplicative mask does not exclude an interaction—it changes its logit to zero, which still receives positive softmax mass. The text also does not clearly specify the causal mask required for GPT-style attention.

Evaluation: The central latency claims are not supported by a sufficiently described real distributed experiment. The paper says inference is “simulated” on laptops with bandwidth caps but omits topology, transport and collective implementations, network latency, serialization, synchronization, communication overlap, quantization/codebook-lookup timing, warm-up, and latency variance. Reporting only means over 20 runs is insufficient for claims such as 2.64× over one device and up to 15.25× over the strongest baseline, especially under emulated rather than variable real Wi-Fi conditions.

Evaluation fairness and significance: Comparisons are almost entirely against full-precision communication. There is no sequence-parallel baseline with ordinary 8-bit/4-bit activation quantization, another learned communication codec, or a quality-matched compression method. Consequently, the results establish that transmitting 10–320-bit indices is cheaper than transmitting float32 embeddings, but do not convincingly establish superiority over competitive communication-compressed alternatives. Actual network traffic also depends on device count and collective topology, which the reported “total bits per token” metric obscures.

Generality: GPT evaluation accelerates only prompt encoding; the manuscript explicitly returns autoregressive decoding to one device. No end-to-end generation latency, time-to-first-token versus inter-token-latency breakdown, or generated-text quality is reported. ViT-Base and GPT-2 Small/Medium are also too limited to support broad claims about deployment of modern large Transformer models.

Accuracy evidence: Language-model degradation is material. GPT2-Medium zero-shot perplexity rises from 43.22 to 62.29 even with 32 groups, and the one-group setting rises to 96.99. The paper reframes fine-tuned PPL gaps as small percentage increases in log loss, which understates their practical magnitude. Results use the best commitment weight but provide no independent model-selection protocol, multiple seeds, confidence intervals, or statistical tests.

Originality: Combining sequence parallelism with per-layer vector quantization is sensible, and residual-noise training plus replicated class tokens are potentially useful refinements, but each ingredient is conceptually straightforward. The narrow related-work treatment and absence of compressed-communication baselines make it difficult to determine how much is fundamentally new rather than an integration of known sequence parallelism, grouped VQ, noise regularization, and ensemble-style averaging.

Reproducibility and presentation: The promised open-source URL is blank. Essential training details—learning rate, batch size, schedule, preprocessing, random seeds, K-means sampling and initialization, EMA settings, and residual-covariance estimation—are missing, as are baseline implementation and network-emulation details. There are also visible signs of insufficient proofreading, including inconsistent headline speedups, malformed appendix text (“r[htb]”), incomplete reference information, and ambiguous terminology such as “Datasize per Token.”

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important bottleneck: communication-dominated Transformer inference on bandwidth-constrained devices. Combining sequence partitioning with vector-quantized remote representations is intuitive, useful, and moderately original.

The evaluation spans ViT-Base, GPT-2 Small/Medium, vision and language datasets, 2–8 devices, 10–500 Mbps bandwidth, and sequence lengths up to 4096. The reported latency advantage is substantial, including a 2.64× single-device speedup in the highlighted low-bandwidth setting.

ASTRA exposes a meaningful accuracy–communication tradeoff. For example, 32-group VQ retains 80.05% versus 80.32% ImageNet accuracy at 76.8× compression, while the device-count study shows only a gradual accuracy decline.

The ablations provide empirical support for the proposed accuracy-preservation components: noise augmentation improves CIFAR-100 validation accuracy by 0.86 points, and distributed class tokens consistently outperform a single class token.

The main method and experiments are generally organized clearly, and the limitations section honestly identifies degraded zero-shot language-model generalization and codebook-storage costs. The societal-impact discussion appropriately notes reliability risks in distributed deployments.
weaknesses: The two theoretical results are not sound as stated. Theorem 1 applies the Gaussian Wasserstein formula without assuming that the embedding distributions are Gaussian and asserts CX=C_hatX+Sigma while omitting cross-covariance between the quantized embedding and its residual. Its strict inequality also needs nondegeneracy conditions. In Theorem 2, softmax perturbations are incorrectly described as mutually independent, errors across device-specific class tokens need not be independent because they derive from shared tokens/codebooks, and the derivation confuses numbers of non-local tokens with output coordinates. Consequently, neither claimed equality is established.

The systems evidence is insufficiently documented for the paper's strongest practical claims. The manuscript says inference is simulated on laptops with 1660Ti GPUs and bandwidth caps, but does not specify whether communication occurred among physical machines, the network topology/protocol, latency and synchronization costs, collective implementation, warm-up procedure, or how each baseline was implemented and tuned. Reporting means over 20 runs without dispersion further limits confidence.

Accuracy and latency are mostly reported separately, making the headline speedups difficult to interpret at matched quality. The fastest G=1 configuration has appreciable degradation—such as ImageNet accuracy falling from 80.32% to 77.12% and GPT-2 Medium zero-shot perplexity rising from 43.22 to 96.99—while exact-computation baselines preserve outputs. A Pareto comparison under common accuracy constraints is needed.

The language-model result accelerates only prompt digestion; autoregressive decoding then moves to one device. There is no end-to-end generation benchmark varying output length, so the broad claim of accelerating GPT-2 inference is stronger than the presented evidence.

Reproducibility is weak. Although the abstract says ASTRA is open-sourced, no repository URL is provided. Important details are absent, including learning rates, batch sizes, preprocessing, random seeds or confidence intervals, the precise Wikipedia corpus/split, residual-statistics estimation, codebook initialization/update schedules, and communication software.

The evaluation is limited to relatively small, older models on homogeneous GPUs. Heterogeneous devices, fluctuating wireless links, failures, memory/storage overhead, energy use, and modern large-model or KV-cache workloads are not evaluated, reducing the demonstrated deployment significance.

The manuscript is readable overall, but several equations and statements need correction or clarification—for example the role of the mask in Equation 1, whether communication totals include replication to all peers, and the claim that ASTRA preserves the original architecture despite requiring task-specific fine-tuning and added per-layer codebooks. These issues prevent reliable acceptance in the current form despite the promising core idea.

The evaluation spans ViT, GPT-2, and Llama-3-8B; vision and language tasks; multiple device counts, sequence lengths, bandwidths, compression levels, and model-quantization settings. The ablations separately examine noise augmentation, distributed class tokens, commitment weight, and codebook size.

The paper is clearly organized and candidly identifies important limitations, including degraded zero-shot generalization, required fine-tuning, device-count-specific adaptation, and acceleration of LLM prefill rather than autoregressive decoding.

The accuracy results show that grouped VQ can closely preserve in-domain ViT performance: with 32 groups, ImageNet accuracy is 80.28% versus 80.32% for the original model. The distributed-class-token ablation also shows consistent empirical gains.
The societal-impact discussion appropriately notes reliability, synchronization, debugging, and safety-critical deployment concerns; no unresolved ethical issue independently prevents acceptance.
weaknesses: The central end-to-end latency evidence appears internally inconsistent. Table 1 defines 3,840 communicated bits per token for the 12-layer ViT at G=32, so 1,024 tokens require 3,932,160 bits and therefore about 39.3 ms at 100 Mbps before collective-protocol effects. Table 15 instead reports 3.27 ms—exactly the cost of 320 bits per token for one layer. This apparent omission of the factor of 12 directly undermines the headline speedups and the claim that communication has ceased to be the bottleneck. The paper provides no latency formula or implementation detail that could reconcile the discrepancy.

The systems evaluation is insufficiently specified and validated. It says distributed inference is simulated on laptops with bandwidth caps, but does not explain the communication backend, topology, synchronization, message framing, collective implementation, serialization, latency injection, warm-up, number of timing trials, variance, or whether communication and computation overlap. Consequently, the reported real-world and end-to-end conclusions are not reproducible or convincingly supported.

Theorem 3.1 is invalid as stated. The proof applies the closed-form Gaussian Wasserstein formula without assuming that X and its quantized distribution are Gaussian. It also asserts C_X = C_Xhat + Sigma, omitting cross-covariance terms between the quantized vector and its residual. The theorem states a strict inequality despite degenerate counterexamples, and assumptions such as isotropic Gaussian residuals appear only inside the proof. Moreover, the injected noise is removed at inference, limiting the theorem's relevance to the claimed deployed model.

Theorem 3.2 likewise does not establish its claimed exact 1/N error reduction. Softmax perturbations are correlated because every delta-alpha shares the same normalization term, contradicting the proof's independence claim. Errors from distributed class tokens also share tokens, codebooks, and quantized representations and therefore are not generally independent across devices. The derivation further confuses the number of non-local tokens with independent coordinates and moves from loose first-order variance bounds to an exact equality without justification.

The accuracy evidence does not compensate for the unsupported latency claim. Some degradation is substantial: GPT2-M zero-shot perplexity rises from 43.22 to 62.29 even at G=32, while Llama-3-8B at G=1 rises from 5.81 to 7.73; SST-2 accuracy drops from 84.26% to 75.45%. Describing these outcomes broadly as preserving accuracy or as minor differences is overstated.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite reporting a seed and coarse epoch counts. The manuscript supplies no code or artifact, and omits essential training and implementation details such as learning rates, batch sizes, schedules, preprocessing, exact checkpoints, codebook-update parameters, quantization kernels, and baseline configurations. Reporting only aggregate ten-seed ImageNet statistics is not enough to reproduce the full study.

The originality is moderate rather than exceptional: sequence parallelism, vector quantization, residual-noise augmentation, and replicated/averaged class tokens are mostly established ingredients. Their combination is useful, but the claimed theoretical novelty and systems significance depend on analyses that are presently unsound.

Overall, the paper has a promising specialized idea and broad experiments, but the apparent layer-count error in communication latency and invalid theoretical guarantees are decisive soundness problems. Corrected end-to-end measurements on an actual distributed implementation and substantially revised theory are necessary before others can reliably build on the contribution.

The evaluation is broad in nominal scope, covering ViT-Base, GPT-2, and Llama-3-8B; vision and language tasks; multiple bandwidths, sequence lengths, device counts, quantization levels, and several ablations.

The reported communication reductions and low-bandwidth latency results are potentially useful. The accuracy/communication trade-off is exposed through the number of VQ groups rather than hidden behind one operating point.

The paper candidly acknowledges several important limitations, including poor zero-shot generalization, prefill-only acceleration for decoder models, fine-tuning requirements, and separate adaptation for different device counts. Its appendix also discusses distributed-system reliability risks.
weaknesses: Soundness: Theorem 3.1 is invalid as stated. The proof assumes Cov(X)=Cov(X-hat)+Cov(epsilon), omitting cross-covariance terms between the quantized value and its residual. It also applies the closed-form Gaussian Wasserstein formula although X and X-hat are not assumed Gaussian. Matching residual mean and covariance with Gaussian noise does not establish the claimed Wasserstein inequality, and the asserted strict inequality can fail in degenerate cases.

Soundness: Theorem 3.2 likewise does not justify its exact 1/N error reduction. Quantization errors need not be zero-mean or mutually independent; softmax perturbations share a normalization term and hence are not independent; errors across devices depend on overlapping tokens; and Equation 33 appears to confuse the number of non-local tokens with the dimensionality of the attention-output error. At most, the derivation suggests a heuristic first-order variance argument under strong assumptions.

The central latency evidence is insufficiently specified. The manuscript says distributed inference is simulated on laptops with bandwidth caps, but does not describe the network topology, collective implementations, transport protocol, synchronization, communication/computation overlap, batch size, warm-up, number of timing trials, variance, or whether communication latency is measured or analytically added. This makes the large speedup claims difficult to validate.

Comparisons are not accuracy-matched. The fastest ASTRA configurations incur substantial degradation—for example, GPT2-M zero-shot perplexity rises from 43.22 to 96.99 at one group, while Llama-3-8B perplexity rises from 5.81 to 7.73. Latency tables nevertheless compare these variants directly with exact baselines, without presenting a controlled latency-quality Pareto comparison. Calling some of these changes “small” or “close” understates their practical magnitude.

The non-ideal-network evidence is weak. The 5% packet-loss experiment does not explain the transport or how missing indices are handled, and its perplexity occasionally improves under loss. The dynamic-bandwidth result uses a synthetic Markov trace, but request arrival, scheduling, batching, and throughput methodology are not specified; it therefore does not support strong claims about realistic robustness.

Reproducibility is inadequate despite reporting some seed statistics. No code or artifact is identified, and essential details such as learning rates, batch sizes, preprocessing, codebook initialization sample sizes, residual-covariance estimation, communication implementation, baseline tuning, and latency measurement procedure are absent. The Llama communication accounting also appears different from the earlier embedding-quantization description and is not fully reconciled.

Originality is moderate: combining sequence parallelism with vector-quantized activation exchange is intuitive, while noise injection and replicated class tokens are incremental adaptations. The related evaluation omits sufficiently close activation/communication-compression and approximate-attention baselines, so the advantage attributable to the specific innovations is unclear.

The practical reach is narrower than the framing suggests: every device stores a full model, decoder-only models receive no decode-phase acceleration, and deployment requires fine-tuning separate variants for different device counts. These limitations are honestly disclosed, but materially weaken the claimed broad applicability to edge and consumer hardware.

Presentation is generally readable, but several claims are overstated relative to the evidence, and the main Impact Statement says no consequences require highlighting even though the appendix itself identifies reliability and safety-critical deployment concerns. The invalid formal results and incomplete experimental description require major revision before others could reliably build on the work.

strengths: Soundness/significance: ASTRA addresses an important practical bottleneck—layer-wise communication under 10–100 Mbps links—by combining sequence parallelism with vector-quantized non-local representations. The resulting latency–accuracy trade-off is useful: on four devices it reports up to 2.64× speedup over single-device inference, while the 32-group ViT variant nearly matches ImageNet accuracy (80.28% versus 80.32%).

Evaluation breadth is strong. The paper covers ViT-Base, GPT-2 Small/Medium, and Llama-3-8B; vision and language tasks; 2–8 devices; 256–4096 tokens; multiple bandwidths; heterogeneous token allocations; model quantization; packet loss; and dynamic-bandwidth traces. Component, codebook-size, commitment-weight, and multi-seed ablations provide useful supporting evidence.

Originality: mixed-precision local/non-local attention is a compelling adaptation of vector quantization to distributed inference. Noise-augmented quantization and distributed class tokens are sensible mechanisms for recovering accuracy, with ablations showing gains of up to 0.86 and 7.13 percentage points, respectively.

Presentation is generally clear and well organized. The diagrams and latency breakdowns communicate the system intuition effectively, and the paper distinguishes communication compression from ordinary weight or KV-cache compression.

The authors candidly identify meaningful limitations: degraded zero-shot performance, fine-tuning and device-count-specific adaptation, prefill-only acceleration for generative models, and distributed-system reliability concerns. The societal-impact discussion is adequate and raises no unresolved material ethical issue.
weaknesses: The theoretical results are not sound as stated. Theorem 3.1 applies the Gaussian closed-form Wasserstein expression although the quantized distribution is discrete and never assumes both distributions are Gaussian; it also asserts Cov(X)=Cov(X̂)+Σ while omitting cross-covariance terms. Consequently, the claimed strict distributional improvement does not follow in general.

Theorem 3.2 likewise relies on unrealistic or internally incorrect independence claims. Softmax perturbations share a normalization term and are not mutually independent, while class-token errors across devices reuse the same quantized tokens and are generally correlated. The proof also confuses non-local-token count with output coordinates. Thus the exact 1/N error reduction is unsupported, although the empirical class-token ablation remains valuable.

Reproducibility is only moderate. The paper provides epochs, a seed, and broad hardware information, but no code-release statement and insufficient detail on learning rates, schedules, preprocessing, collective implementation, topology, synchronization, serialization, warm-up/repetition protocol, or latency variance. These details materially affect systems results.

Baseline comparability needs strengthening. Block Parallelism changes the architecture, yet its accuracy for the aggressively accelerated Nb=1 and Nb=4 configurations is not reported. Latency comparisons therefore do not establish an accuracy-matched advantage. The manuscript also ambiguously describes distributed execution as being “simulated” on laptops.

Several robustness and scalability claims need better specification. The 5% packet-loss experiment does not explain packet granularity or how missing indices are handled, and its near-zero effect is surprising without retransmission. The Llama implementation also appears to quantize K/V representations with different dimensional accounting from the embedding-level method described earlier, but this variant is not clearly documented.

The accuracy cost is nontrivial outside vision: GPT-2 Medium zero-shot perplexity rises from 43.22 to 62.29 even with 32 groups, and some Llama downstream drops are substantial (e.g., SST-2 from 84.26% to 75.45% at one group). This limits claims of broadly preserving model quality and makes workload-specific tuning necessary.
